idiom_name: package directory with __init__.py as the published surface; __all__ and underscore names for internals
implementation_notes: A Python module is a .py file and a package is a directory with __init__.py; the package namespace is the published surface, so the __init__.py decides what clients see - importing the intended names and listing them in __all__ documents the interface, while names with a leading underscore and submodules that are not imported there remain internal by convention. Nothing is enforced: any client can import billing._ledger, so the boundary rests on discipline, and __all__ affects only `from package import *`. A domain module is one package per domain area with a thin __init__.py re-exporting its entities, value objects and services.
code_sketch:
# billing/__init__.py - the module's published surface
from .invoice import Invoice
from .money import Money

__all__ = ["Invoice", "Money"]

# billing/_ledger.py - internal by convention
# clients: from billing import Invoice
pitfalls: Underscore privacy is only a convention: from billing._ledger import ... works and tooling autocompletes internals.
__init__.py runs at import time, so heavy imports or side effects there turn the module boundary into startup cost and can create circular-import failures.
Module names compete on sys.path: a billing.py next to a billing/ package, or a stdlib name, silently shadows or is shadowed.
Circular imports fail at run time with partially initialised modules, so dependency direction has to be checked by a linter rather than by the interpreter.

variants.name: Namespace package (PEP 420)
variants.implementation_notes: Since Python 3.3 a directory without __init__.py is a namespace package: the import machinery merges portions of the same package found on different sys.path entries, so one domain module may be distributed across several wheels or repositories. There is no single __init__.py to hold the published surface, so the interface is expressed by the submodule names and documentation instead; use it for split distribution, not for ordinary domain modelling, where the regular package states the boundary more clearly.
variants.code_sketch:
# no __init__.py in billing/
# distribution A provides billing/core/invoice.py
# distribution B provides billing/reports/invoice_report.py

from billing.core.invoice import Invoice      # merged namespace
pitfalls: A namespace package cannot carry the __init__ re-exports that normally define the published surface, so the interface degrades into a naming convention.
Portions are resolved through sys.path order, so one distribution can silently shadow or extend another distribution's portion of the package.
